enrichment.short_title: Date of service of section 25 notice by recorded delivery
key_facts: The landlord served a section 25 notice by recorded delivery on 7 January 2002; the tenant received it on 9 January 2002.
The tenant served a counter-notice and applied for a new tenancy on 8 May 2002, within four months of actual receipt but arguably out of time if service was deemed on posting.
The parties agreed the deemed date of service should be determined as a preliminary issue.
Neuberger J held that service by recorded delivery under section 23 of the 1927 Act is irrebuttably deemed on the date of posting, not receipt.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Landlord's appeal from a county court preliminary issue decision that the tenant's new tenancy application was in time.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the section 25 notice was deemed served on 7 January 2002 and the tenant's application was out of time.
enrichment.ratio: Where a notice under the 1954 Act is sent by recorded delivery to the addressee at his place of abode, section 23 of the 1927 Act (incorporated by section 66(4)) irrebuttably deems service on the date of posting; section 7 of the Interpretation Act 1978 does not displace that effect, and construing section 23 otherwise would not engage the Human Rights Act.
legal_issues: Whether service by recorded delivery is deemed on posting or on receipt
Whether section 7 of the Interpretation Act 1978 applies to section 23 service
Whether Chiswell, Galinski, Railtrack and Mustapha or Lex Service governs
Whether irrebuttable deemed service infringes the tenant's human rights

enrichment.short_title: Small claims costs where claim never allocated to track
key_facts: The claimant sued for return of a video card; the pleaded claim exceeded £5,000 but the true value was £2,502.43 after a dollars/pounds error was conceded.
Default judgments were entered and later set aside; the case proceeded to a disposal hearing without ever being allocated to a track.
The district judge awarded £6,000 costs, holding that the small claims regime did not apply because no allocation order had been made.
The Court of Appeal held that absence of allocation was not conclusive and remitted costs for assessment on the small claims basis.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from Brentford County Court on the costs order made at a disposal hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; costs up to 13 June 2001 remitted to the district judge for decision on the small claims regime unless agreed.
enrichment.ratio: Treating the absence of a track allocation order as conclusive is a misdirection; where a claim was in substance a small claim and would inevitably have been allocated to the small claims track, the normal rule is that the Part 27 costs limitations apply, consistent with the discretionary and proportionate approach to costs.
legal_issues: Whether the small claims costs regime applies without a formal allocation order
Whether the district judge misdirected himself by treating lack of allocation as determinative
Whether the Court of Appeal should interfere with a costs discretion
Whether a second appeal was justified on a point of principle

confidence.notes: Clear procedural point of principle with detailed procedural history and unanimous Court of Appeal decision.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum judicial review and expert report on Basij membership
key_facts: An Iranian claimant sought asylum on the basis of unorthodox religious views and alleged Basij membership exposing him to persecution.
The adjudicator found the Basij account fabricated and that local difficulties with a religious teacher amounted to discrimination, not persecution.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused permission to appeal; the claimant sought judicial review.
Mr Joffe's expert report assumed the claimant's account was true and did not corroborate the disputed Basij membership findings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of the adjudicator's asylum dismissal and the IAT's refusal of permission to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the adjudicator's credibility and persecution findings were unassailable.
enrichment.ratio: An expert country report that merely assumes the appellant's account and addresses risk on that counterfactual basis does not corroborate disputed primary facts; where the adjudicator has rejected the appellant's story as fabricated, failure expressly to accept or reject such a report does not constitute an error of law.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator erred in failing to engage with Mr Joffe's expert report
Whether the report corroborated the claimant's Basij membership account
Whether risk on return as a failed asylum seeker was raised before the adjudicator
Standard of review of adjudicator credibility findings

confidence.notes: Straightforward judicial review on expert evidence and fact-finding; grounds clearly addressed.

enrichment.short_title: Deemed consent for illuminated Coldharbour Lane hoarding

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Control of Advertisements) Regulations 1992
Town and Country Planning (Control of Advertisement) Regulations 1948

key_facts: Lambeth sought to remove an advertising hoarding at 220–224 Coldharbour Lane under section 11 of the 1995 Act, claiming no express or deemed consent.
Express consent granted in 1956 had expired in 1959; the site had been used continuously for advertisements since then.
Illumination bars were added in 1989; Lambeth's enforcement process was heavily criticised for improper demands and premature notices.
Collins J held Class 14 deemed consent applied because the 1956 consent, read with the statutory definition of advertisement, permitted illuminated use.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review challenge to section 11 removal notices served by Lambeth London Borough Council.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; the section 11 notices were quashed.
enrichment.ratio: Class 14 deemed consent continues where a site has been used continually for the purpose permitted by expired express consent; illumination added after expiry does not necessarily remove that consent if the original consent, construed with the wide definition of advertisement in the 1990 Act, did not restrict illumination, and a breach of a Class 13 condition may be remedied rather than permanently destroying deemed consent.
legal_issues: Whether Class 14 deemed consent survived addition of illumination in 1989
Construction of 'used for the purpose' in Class 14(2)
Whether Class 13 deemed consent was lost by substantial alteration in manner of use
Lawfulness of Lambeth's section 11 enforcement procedure and burden of proof

enrichment.short_title: Stay of noise prosecution for late CPIA disclosure
key_facts: Warren Elias was prosecuted for breaching a noise abatement notice at 77 Laleham Road; his defence blamed noise from the neighbouring Dartmouth Hotel.
Lewisham failed to disclose until mid-trial material about prior pub noise complaints, an abatement notice and cautions.
The district judge stayed the prosecution as an abuse of process, finding actual prejudice after the prosecution case had closed.
The Divisional Court upheld the stay, though noting adjournment might sometimes cure late disclosure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Prosecutor's appeal by way of case stated from Marylebone Magistrates' Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the stay for abuse of process was lawful.
enrichment.ratio: Material showing prior noise nuisance from a neighbouring pub was capable of assisting the defence and should have been disclosed under section 7 CPIA 1996 before trial; although the trial process can often cure late disclosure, a district judge may lawfully stay proceedings as an abuse where prejudice cannot now be remedied.
legal_issues: Whether undisclosed pub noise material was capable of assisting the defence
Whether late secondary disclosure amounted to abuse of process
Whether the district judge should have adjourned rather than stayed
Appropriate use of the stay jurisdiction in summary trials

enrichment.short_title: Challenge to MHRT discharge of Ashworth patient
key_facts: Patient D, detained at Ashworth Hospital under section 3, was discharged by the Mental Health Review Tribunal with a one-month deferral for aftercare.
Mersey Care NHS Trust challenged the decision as irrational, inadequately reasoned and procedurally unfair.
Written reports favoured continued detention, but oral evidence showed substantial improvement and day-to-day staff supported community care with a package.
Sullivan J refused judicial review and declined to set aside the discharge; the stay was lifted in effect.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent application for judicial review with interim stay of the Tribunal's discharge decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; the Tribunal's decision to discharge was lawful.
enrichment.ratio: A Mental Health Review Tribunal exercising its original jurisdiction may rationally order discharge where up-to-date oral evidence, including from ward staff and the patient, supports community coping with medication compliance and a deferred aftercare package, even if earlier written reports recommended continued detention; brief reasons may be amplified by witness statements where liberty is at stake.
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal's discharge decision was irrational against unanimous medical evidence
Adequacy of the Tribunal's reasons for discharge
Procedural fairness regarding the RMO's ability to question witnesses and sum up
Whether an adequate community care package could be arranged within one month

enrichment.short_title: Guardian's section 42 access after foster carer arrest

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Court Services Act 2000

key_facts: Baby S was in foster care when his foster father was arrested in Operation Ore; the local authority removed S and misled the mother and magistrates about the reason.
On 17 October 2002 the authority told the justices S remained with the same foster carers and sought an interim care order on that basis.
The children's guardian later discovered the deception and sought full local authority records under section 42, including an independent inquiry report.
Wall J held the guardian was entitled to all section 42 documents and strongly criticised the authority's conduct.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application in care proceedings for disclosure of local authority records under section 42 of the Children Act 1989.
enrichment.outcome: Guardian granted access to Mrs AH's report and all relevant section 42 records; local authority ordered to pay the guardian's disclosure costs.
enrichment.ratio: A CAFCASS officer appointed under section 41 has a broad statutory right under section 42 to examine local authority records relating to the child, including inquiry reports commissioned because of the authority's conduct in the proceedings; public interest immunity does not override section 42, and local authorities must cooperate fully and be frank with the court in care proceedings.
legal_issues: Scope of section 42 rights to local authority records
Whether PII or foster-carer confidentiality limits guardian access
Whether Mrs AH's independent inquiry report 'relates to' the child
Local authority duty of frankness to the court in care proceedings

confidence.notes: Authoritative published judgment on section 42 with detailed factual background and clear legal ruling.

enrichment.short_title: Retrospective costs cap in organ retention GLO
key_facts: The Nationwide Organ Group Litigation concerned claims over retention of organs by NHS hospitals, with about 369 registered claims and four lead cases.
Claimants' generic costs had already reached £1.45 million; further costs of about £1 million were estimated to trial.
The defendants sought a novel retrospective and prospective costs cap from 10 February 2003 through trial.
Gage J held the court had power to cap costs and set a global cap of £506,500 for claimants' generic costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application in group litigation for a retrospective and prospective costs cap order at case management stage.
enrichment.outcome: Costs cap order made for £506,500 from 10 February 2003 to end of trial, based on a four-week trial estimate.
enrichment.ratio: The court has power under CPR case management provisions and section 51 to make a costs cap order in group litigation to keep costs proportionate; the cap should be assessed broadly by component parts—solicitors, counsel, experts and disbursements—and need not require exceptional circumstances in a GLO.
legal_issues: Whether the court has jurisdiction to make a retrospective costs cap order
How to assess a proportionate global costs cap in a GLO
Appropriate hourly rates and hours for claimants' solicitors
Relationship between claimants' agreed LSC case plans and the court's cap

enrichment.short_title: No English habeas corpus jurisdiction over Scottish extradition
key_facts: Mr Wright and Mr Brown were in Scottish custody facing extradition to Estonia for drug trafficking offences.
They applied to the English Divisional Court for habeas corpus, arguing Scottish detainees lacked an equivalent remedy.
Authority to proceed was issued in March 2001 and Sheriff Bell committed them in custody pending ministerial decision.
The court held the English writ does not run in Scotland and section 11(6) provides review in the High Court of Justiciary instead.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to the Divisional Court for habeas corpus or equivalent relief concerning Scottish extradition committals.
enrichment.outcome: Application rejected as misconceived; no jurisdiction to review Sheriff Bell's committal.
enrichment.ratio: The Extradition Act 1989 applies throughout the United Kingdom but provides separate remedies: habeas corpus in England and review in the High Court of Justiciary in Scotland; Article XIX of the Act of Union 1706 prevents English courts reviewing or stopping execution of Scottish judicial acts.
legal_issues: Whether the English writ of habeas corpus runs in Scotland
Effect of section 11(6) Extradition Act 1989 in Scotland
Whether a lacuna in Scottish remedies confers English jurisdiction
Whether committal by a Sheriff rather than Sheriff Principal was defective

enrichment.short_title: Section 73 certification of late human rights claim
key_facts: A Sri Lankan claimant's asylum and human rights appeals were dismissed; he later relied on a fresh psychiatric report to resist removal.
Dr Coleman's 2002 report raised severe depression, PTSD and suicide risk if returned, supporting Article 3 and Article 8 claims.
The Secretary of State certified the appeal under section 73 as raising grounds that could have been made earlier and for delay.
Mitting J upheld the certification but granted permission to appeal on the proper construction of section 73.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's section 73 certificate treating further human rights grounds as finally determined.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; permission to appeal granted on interpretation of section 73.
enrichment.ratio: In section 73, 'claim' and 'grounds' mean the combined factual and legal basis for contending removal would breach human rights; 'no other legitimate purpose' is a long-stop safeguard and does not require the claim to be hopeless; certification is discretionary and the Secretary of State properly considered new psychiatric material when certifying Article 8 grounds that could reasonably have been raised in the original human rights appeal.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'claim' and 'grounds' in section 73(2) and (5)
Construction of 'no other legitimate purpose' in section 73(2)(c)
Discretionary factors relevant to issuing a section 73 certificate
Whether Article 8 mental-health removal arguments were certifiable
